title: What an EEG Is Like: Testing for Seizures
teaser: An EEG is a painless test that records your brain's electrical activity to help evaluate seizures. Here's what to expect before, during, and after.
body_html:
If your neurologist has recommended an electroencephalogram — better known as an EEG — it is natural to feel a little unsure about what the day will involve. The good news is that an EEG is a painless, non-invasive test that simply listens to the natural electrical activity of your brain. Nothing is injected, and no electricity is sent into you. For anyone being evaluated for seizures, an EEG is one of the most helpful tools your care team has.

What an EEG Measures

Your brain cells communicate through small electrical signals. An EEG records those signals using sensors, called electrodes, that rest on the surface of your scalp. The activity is displayed as waves that your neurologist can review. Some patterns can point toward epilepsy, help tell seizures apart from other causes of spells or fainting, and guide decisions about treatment. Because the test looks at brain activity as it happens, it offers information that imaging scans cannot.

How to Prepare

Preparation is usually simple. Come with clean, dry hair, and skip conditioner, oils, gels, or hairspray on the day of the test, since these can keep the electrodes from making good contact. Eat normally unless you are told otherwise, and ask whether you should take your usual medications as scheduled. In some cases, your neurologist may request a sleep-deprived EEG, which means getting less sleep the night before so certain patterns are more likely to appear. Our office will give you specific instructions when your test is scheduled.

What Happens During the Test

When you arrive, a technologist will measure your scalp and gently attach the electrodes with a mild paste. This part does not hurt, though the paste can feel a little cool. You will then relax, usually lying down or reclining, while the recording is made. Most EEGs take about an hour, including the setup time.

During the test, you may be asked to do a few simple things that can bring out brain patterns. These often include opening and closing your eyes, breathing deeply for a few minutes, and looking at a flashing light. If any of these feel uncomfortable, tell the technologist — you are always in control. Many people find the experience calm enough that they doze off, which is perfectly fine and can even be helpful.

After Your EEG

Once the recording is finished, the electrodes are removed and any leftover paste can be washed out at home. There is no recovery time, and you can return to your normal daily activities, unless your neurologist has advised otherwise. A specialist reviews the recording, and your physician will explain what the results mean at a follow-up visit, along with any next steps in your care.

Talk With a Neurologist

An EEG is one piece of a larger picture. At Palm Beach Neurology & Premiere Research Institute, our physicians use it alongside your history and other testing to understand what is happening and to build a plan that fits you. If you have questions about seizures, spells, or an upcoming EEG, we are here to help. Learn more about epilepsy & seizures, or request an appointment at our West Palm Beach office. You can also reach us at 561-845-0500.

This article is general information and not medical advice. For any specific concern, please talk with your physician. If you are having a medical emergency, or a seizure lasts more than five minutes, call 911.

title: EMG & Nerve Conduction: Finding the Source of Numbness
teaser: Numbness, tingling, or weakness that won't quit? See how EMG and nerve conduction studies help our West Palm Beach neurologists find the cause.
body_html:
Numbness, tingling, or a hand or foot that feels weak or "asleep" can be unsettling, especially when it does not go away. Sensations like these often begin in the nerves and muscles, and one of the most useful ways to understand them is a pair of tests done together: electromyography (EMG) and a nerve conduction study (NCS). At Palm Beach Neurology & Premiere Research Institute, our neurologists use these studies to look beneath the surface and pinpoint the source of the problem.

What an EMG & Nerve Conduction Study Measures

Although they are usually performed in the same visit, the two tests look at different things. A nerve conduction study measures how quickly and how strongly electrical signals travel along a nerve. Small sensors are placed on the skin, and a gentle pulse stimulates the nerve so we can time its response. An EMG then looks at the muscles themselves. Using a very thin needle electrode, it records the natural electrical activity a muscle produces at rest and when you gently contract it. Together, they help us tell whether a nerve, a muscle, or the connection between them is involved.

Why Your Neurologist May Recommend One

These tests are often suggested when symptoms point toward a problem in the peripheral nerves or muscles. They can help clarify the cause of numbness, tingling, burning, cramping, or weakness, and they are commonly used to evaluate conditions such as peripheral neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, pinched nerves in the neck or back, and a range of neuromuscular disorders. Rather than guessing, the results give your physician objective information about which nerves or muscles are affected and how significantly.

What to Expect During the Test

An EMG and nerve conduction study is done right in our West Palm Beach office and usually takes somewhere between 30 and 60 minutes, depending on how many nerves or muscles need to be checked. During the nerve conduction portion, you will feel brief, mild electrical pulses, similar to a quick tap or a small static shock. During the EMG portion, you may feel a small pinch as the thin electrode is placed. Most people find the study very manageable. You can eat normally beforehand, and it helps to wear comfortable clothing and to let us know if you take blood thinners or have a pacemaker so we can plan accordingly.

Making Sense of Your Results

After the study, your neurologist reviews the recordings and combines them with your history and physical exam. The findings can show whether a nerve is compressed, whether nerve fibers are irritated or damaged, and whether the pattern fits a localized issue or something more widespread. That clarity guides the next steps, whether that means further testing, a treatment plan, or simply reassurance. Physicians on our team, including specialists in nerve and muscle conditions, perform and interpret these studies as part of a complete neurological evaluation.

Talk With Our West Palm Beach Team

If numbness, tingling, or weakness has been bothering you, you do not have to keep wondering what is behind it. Our physicians have spent 25+ years caring for the Palm Beaches, and we are accepting new patients. Request an appointment to discuss your symptoms and find out whether an EMG and nerve conduction study is right for you. You can also explore our on-site clinical research program, which studies conditions that affect the nerves and brain.

This article is general information, not medical advice. For guidance about your own health, please speak with a physician. If you are having a medical emergency, call 911.

title: Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's: The Basics
teaser: Deep brain stimulation can ease Parkinson's tremor, stiffness, and slowness. Learn how DBS works, who it may help, and what to expect, in plain English.
body_html:
If you or someone you love is living with Parkinson's disease, you may have heard the term "deep brain stimulation," or DBS. It can sound intimidating at first, but the idea behind it is fairly straightforward. This article walks through the basics in plain English so you can have a more informed conversation with your neurologist.

What Is Deep Brain Stimulation?

Deep brain stimulation is a treatment that uses gentle electrical impulses to help regulate the brain signals involved in movement. During a procedure performed by a neurosurgeon, thin wires called leads are placed in specific areas of the brain that help control motor function. These leads connect to a small device, similar in concept to a heart pacemaker, that sits under the skin near the collarbone. The device sends carefully tuned signals that can help calm some of the movement problems Parkinson's causes.

DBS is not a cure, and it does not stop Parkinson's from progressing. Instead, it is a tool that can help manage symptoms and, for the right person, improve day-to-day quality of life.

Which Symptoms Can It Help?

DBS is best known for easing the movement-related symptoms of Parkinson's, including tremor, stiffness, and slowness of movement. For many people, it can also reduce the involuntary movements, called dyskinesia, that sometimes come with long-term Parkinson's medication. In some cases, DBS allows a person to lower their medication dose, which may cut down on side effects.

It is worth knowing that DBS tends to help symptoms that already respond, at least somewhat, to medication. Symptoms that do not improve with medication are less likely to change with stimulation.

Who Might Be a Candidate?

DBS is generally considered for people whose Parkinson's symptoms are no longer well controlled by medication alone, or who struggle with medication side effects or symptoms that come and go throughout the day. It is not the right first step for everyone, and it is usually not the first treatment tried. Deciding whether DBS makes sense involves a careful evaluation by a movement-disorders specialist, who will weigh your symptoms, overall health, and personal goals.

What Happens After the Device Is Placed?

The surgery is only part of the process. After the device is implanted and you have had time to heal, a neurologist begins "programming" it, fine-tuning the strength and pattern of the electrical signals to match your needs. This is done in the office, is adjustable, and often takes several visits to get right. Your settings can be updated over time as your symptoms change. At Palm Beach Neurology & Premiere Research Institute, DBS programming is one of the services our movement-disorders team provides.

Talk With a Movement-Disorders Specialist

Every person's Parkinson's journey is different, and the decision about whether DBS is a good fit is a personal one made together with your care team. If you would like to learn more about DBS or about managing Parkinson's and other movement disorders, our team is here to help. You can also explore ongoing clinical research at our on-site Premiere Research Institute. To ask questions or get started, request an appointment or call our West Palm Beach office at 561-845-0500.

This article is for general information only and is not medical advice. For guidance about your own health, please talk with a qualified clinician. If you are experiencing a medical emergency, call 911.

title: Concussion: When to See a Neurologist
teaser: Most concussions heal with rest, but some symptoms signal it is time for expert care. Learn the warning signs and when to see a neurologist.
body_html:
A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury, and the word "mild" can be misleading. Most people who have one recover fully within a few weeks with rest and patience. But the brain is complex, and sometimes symptoms linger, worsen, or point to something that deserves a closer look. Knowing the difference between a normal recovery and a warning sign can help you protect your health and your peace of mind.

What Happens During a Concussion

A concussion occurs when a bump, blow, or jolt to the head, or a hit to the body that shakes the head, causes the brain to move rapidly inside the skull. This sudden motion can briefly disrupt the way brain cells communicate. Common causes include falls, sports collisions, car accidents, and everyday mishaps at home or work. You do not have to lose consciousness to have a concussion. In fact, most people never black out.

Typical symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, sensitivity to light or noise, trouble concentrating, memory fog, irritability, and changes in sleep. These often appear right away, though some can surface hours later.

Warning Signs That Need Emergency Care

Certain symptoms after a head injury are not something to watch and wait on. They call for emergency attention right away. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room if you or someone you are with experiences a severe or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, slurred speech, weakness or numbness in the arms or legs, unequal pupil sizes, extreme confusion or agitation, or difficulty staying awake. In children, watch for persistent crying, refusal to eat, or unusual listlessness. These can be signs of a more serious brain injury that needs urgent evaluation.

When to See a Neurologist

Many concussions improve on their own, but a neurologist's expertise becomes valuable when recovery does not follow the usual path. Consider scheduling an evaluation if your symptoms last longer than a couple of weeks, if headaches become frequent or intense, or if you continue to struggle with dizziness, balance, memory, focus, or mood. This lingering pattern is sometimes called post-concussion syndrome, and it tends to respond best to thoughtful, individualized care.

You should also seek specialized guidance if you have had more than one concussion, if a previous head injury still affects you, or if you simply want the reassurance of a thorough neurological assessment. A neurologist can look at the whole picture, including your history, your symptoms, and how your brain and nervous system are functioning, rather than treating each complaint in isolation.

How a Neurology Practice Can Help

At Palm Beach Neurology & Premiere Research Institute, our physicians evaluate concussion and other forms of traumatic brain injury with a careful, patient-centered approach. Depending on your needs, that may include a detailed neurological exam, cognitive and memory testing, and a plan to address specific symptoms such as persistent headaches, sleep disruption, or difficulty concentrating. The goal is a clear recovery path and steady support along the way.

If you or a loved one is recovering from a head injury and something does not feel right, you do not have to navigate it alone. Our team has cared for the Palm Beaches for more than 25 years, and we are accepting new patients. To talk with us about your symptoms, request an appointment or call our West Palm Beach office at 561-845-0500.

This article is for general information only and is not medical advice. For any emergency, call 911. To discuss your symptoms or schedule a visit, please contact our office at 561-845-0500.

title: Telehealth for Neurology: What Works Remotely
teaser: A plain-English look at which neurology visits work well by video, when an in-person exam is better, and how to prepare — from Palm Beach Neurology.
body_html:
Over the past several years, video visits have become a familiar part of medical care, and neurology is no exception. At Palm Beach Neurology & Premiere Research Institute, we know a trip to the office is not always easy, especially for patients managing memory changes, movement disorders, or frequent headaches. The good news is that a surprising amount of thoughtful neurological care can happen safely over a secure video connection. Knowing what works well remotely, and what still calls for an in-person visit, helps you get the most from every appointment.

What neurology can do well by video

Much of neurology is a conversation. Your neurologist listens carefully to your history, asks detailed questions, and reviews how symptoms have changed over time. That kind of thoughtful exchange translates naturally to a screen. Telehealth tends to work especially well for:

  • Follow-up visits to see how a treatment plan is working and adjust as needed.
  • Medication check-ins for conditions such as migraine, epilepsy, or Parkinson's, where the goal is fine-tuning.
  • Reviewing test results together, so you understand what an EEG, MRI, or blood test means for you.
  • Ongoing headache & migraine management, where tracking triggers and frequency matters as much as a hands-on exam.

Even parts of the neurological exam can be adapted to video. A neurologist can observe your speech, facial movement, tremor, coordination, and how you walk across a room, all of which offer meaningful clues.

When an in-person visit is the better choice

Some care simply needs to happen face to face. A first evaluation for a new or complex problem often benefits from a full, hands-on neurological exam. Testing and procedures we perform in the office, such as EEG, EMG and nerve-conduction studies, Botox for chronic migraine or spasticity, infusion therapy, and deep brain stimulation programming, cannot be done remotely. Detailed cognitive and memory testing may also be more accurate in person.

If your neurologist recommends coming in, it is because certain details are easier to assess directly. Think of telehealth and office visits as partners rather than competitors. Many patients move comfortably between the two over the course of their care.

Getting the most from a video visit

A little preparation goes a long way. Find a quiet, well-lit space where you can speak freely and be seen clearly from head to toe if asked to walk. Have your medication list, a recent symptom or headache diary, and any questions written down. If a family member usually helps at appointments, invite them to join, since an extra set of ears is valuable for memory and movement concerns. Test your internet connection and device beforehand so technical hiccups do not eat into your time.

Telehealth and clinical research

Remote check-ins can also support participation in clinical trials. Through our on-site Premiere Research Institute, some study visits and follow-ups may be handled by phone or video, making it easier to take part in monitored research in areas such as Alzheimer's, migraine, and multiple sclerosis. You can learn more on our clinical research page.

We're here to help

Whether you prefer to meet by video or in our West Palm Beach office, our goal is the same: to help you stay sharp and stay in control. If you are unsure which type of visit is right for you, our team is glad to guide you. Ready to get started? Request an appointment or call us at 561-845-0500, and ask about ongoing headache & migraine care if that is your concern.

This article is for general information only and is not medical advice. For guidance about your own situation, please speak with your neurologist. If you are experiencing a medical emergency, call 911.
